hints: Focus on where caesium and barium sit in Period 6, Group 1 comes just before Group 2 so think about nuclear charge across the period.
Notice that $\text{Cs}^{+}$ and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ both have 54 electrons, so the ion with more protons will pull those electrons in more tightly.
For melting point, compare metallic bonding by thinking about ion charge and number of delocalised electrons donated by a Group 1 versus a Group 2 metal.
walkthrough:
**Locate the elements and their ions**

Caesium is Group 1 so forms $\text{Cs}^{+}$. Barium is Group 2 so forms $\text{Ba}^{2+}$. They are neighbours in Period 6, with barium having one more proton.

Ions: $\text{Cs}^{+}$ has 55 - 1 = 54 electrons, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ has 56 - 2 = 54 electrons

**Compare ionic radius using isoelectronic ions**

Both ions have the same electron arrangement (xenon configuration) and the same number of shells. The key difference is nuclear charge.

$$\text{Ba}^{2+} \text{ has 56 protons, } \text{Cs}^{+} \text{ has 55 protons}$$

**Decide the larger ion**

More protons means stronger attraction for the same number of electrons, so the electrons are drawn closer. That makes $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ smaller than $\text{Cs}^{+}$.

Larger ionic radius: $\text{Cs}^{+}$

**Compare melting point using metallic bonding**

Melting point of a metal depends on strength of metallic bonding, which increases with higher cation charge and more delocalised electrons. Barium provides 2 electrons per atom and forms $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, while caesium provides only 1 electron and forms $\text{Cs}^{+}$.

Higher melting point: barium, a Group 2 metal, is much higher than caesium, a very soft low melting Group 1 metal.

options.A: Incorrect on ionic radius. $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is not larger, even though barium atom has higher atomic number. Because both ions are isoelectronic with 54 electrons, the greater nuclear charge of Ba (56 protons) pulls electrons in more strongly than Cs (55 protons).
options.B: Incorrect on both columns. $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Cs}^{+}$ for the isoelectronic reason above, and caesium does not have the higher melting point. Caesium has only one valence electron and weak metallic bonding, so its melting point is very low.
options.C: Correct on both. $\text{Cs}^{+}$ is larger because with fewer protons holding the same 54 electrons it experiences less nuclear attraction than $\text{Ba}^{2+}$. Barium has the higher melting point because as a Group 2 metal with $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ ions and two delocalised electrons per atom, its metallic bonding is much stronger than that of Group 1 caesium.
options.D: Correct on ionic radius but wrong on melting point. $\text{Cs}^{+}$ is indeed larger, but caesium has a very low melting point (about 28 degrees C). Barium has stronger metallic bonding due to higher charge, so barium melts much higher.
